name: Revenue Mix Shift
description: Revenue held flat or grew, but profit moved because the mix between higher- and lower-margin products shifted.
formula: Profit = Total Volume × [(Mix % A × Contribution Margin A) + (Mix % B × Contribution Margin B)] = Profit_current vs Profit_prior
business_contexts: grocery chain where private-label sales have grown faster than name-brand sales
software company where customers have shifted from premium to entry-level tier
car manufacturer selling more base trims and fewer luxury trims
restaurant chain where combo-meal orders have displaced a la carte orders
telecom provider where customers have shifted from postpaid to prepaid plans
question_patterns: Revenue is flat year over year — why did profit change, and by how much?
How much profit was gained or lost purely from the shift in product mix?
If the mix had stayed the same as last year, what would profit be this year?
What is the dollar impact of customers shifting from Product A to Product B?
solution_logic: Step 3: Calculate prior profit = total_volume × [(mix_pct_a_prior × contribution_margin_a) + (mix_pct_b_prior × contribution_margin_b)]
Step 4: Calculate current profit = total_volume × [(mix_pct_a_current × contribution_margin_a) + (mix_pct_b_current × contribution_margin_b)]
Step 5: Calculate profit delta = current profit - prior profit
key_insight: A flat top line can hide a real profit story — always check what's inside the revenue number before assuming stable revenue means a stable business.
common_mistakes: Assuming flat revenue means flat profit
Averaging the two contribution margins instead of weighting by mix
Forgetting the two mix percentages must sum to 1
framework_soundbite: When revenue looks flat, check what's hiding inside it — mix shifts move profit even when the top line doesn't.
